title: SYSK Selects: Jellyfish - Even Cooler Than Octopi?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on jellyfish and comb jellies. Hosts compare the two groups (Ctenophora vs. Cnidaria), covering body plan, nerve nets, eyes of box jellies, locomotion via cilia versus bell pulsing, and the medusa and polyp life cycle. They discuss the largest species (lion's mane), the Portuguese man of war as a colony, box jellies and the sea wasp, the irukandji jellyfish and its syndrome, stinging nematocysts versus comb jelly glue cells, reproduction (including strobilation and the immortal Turritopsis), jellyfish blooms and their causes (overfishing, nutrient runoff, warming, ocean sprawl), and the Black Sea sea walnut invasion. The episode ends with a listener wedding-anxiety letter.

segments.title: Opening banter and Selects introduction
segments.summary: Hosts open with off-topic banter about jet lag and a secondhand fondue pot, then introduce jellyfish and comb jellies as a favorite sea creature, comparing them to octopus.

segments.title: Jellyfish vs. comb jellies and their body plan
segments.summary: The hosts explain that jellyfish and comb jellies look alike but may not be closely related, then describe the shared body layers, the mesoglea jelly filling, the single body opening, and absorption of nutrients through the skin.

segments.title: Jellyfish eyes, comb jelly cilia, and the polyp and medusa forms
segments.summary: They discuss box jellyfish eyes despite lacking a brain, comb jelly cilia that create a rainbow effect, and the medusa and polyp life stages, including the size of the lion's mane jellyfish.

segments.title: Types of jellyfish: Hydrozoa, Portuguese man of war, Cubozoa, Scyphozoa
segments.summary: The hosts describe the hydrozoa, the Portuguese man of war as a colony of polyps, the cubozoa including the sea wasp, the stalked scyphozoa, and a freshwater jellyfish in the Great Lakes. They also explain how jellyfish move by contracting the bell.

segments.title: Comb jelly types and fossil history
segments.summary: They cover comb jelly groups (cydippids, lobates, beroids) and their feeding, the debate over their relationship, and fossils about five million years old found in Utah, with speculation about which group evolved first.

segments.title: Feeding, predators, and eating jellyfish
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the carnivorous diet, predators such as sea turtles and sunfish, jellyfish eaten as food in China and Japan and a Georgia fishery, and a tangent on flossing.

segments.title: Nematocysts, stings, and Irukandji syndrome
segments.summary: They explain how nematocysts fire venom harpoons versus comb jelly glue cells, describe the tiny Irukandji box jellyfish and its severe symptoms, and address the myth about urinating on stings and using seawater and a credit card to remove tentacles.

segments.title: Bioluminescence, defense, reproduction, and immortality
segments.summary: They cover bioluminescence as defense, camouflage and red pigment in deep-sea jellies, varied reproductive strategies including mass spawning and strobilation, and Turritopsis which can revert to the polyp stage and is considered potentially immortal.

segments.title: Jellyfish blooms, causes, climate change, and the Black Sea invasion
segments.summary: The hosts discuss jellyfish blooms that disrupt power plants and fisheries, possible human causes such as overfishing, nutrient runoff, warming water, and ocean sprawl, and the Black Sea sea walnut invasion that was checked by another jellyfish predator.

segments.title: Listener mail: wedding anxiety
segments.summary: A listener named Stephen writes that the show helped calm his nerves before his wedding.
